title: Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump is arguably the most pro-Israel president of modern times. So hisElection Dayannouncement that the United States would end nearly $4 billionin annual aid to Israelwas stunning.

But as is often the case with Trump, the announcement — made on Fox News — was short on details and difficult to pin down. It could end up being less seismic in practice than the shock announcement might suggest.

Still, Trump’s move was yet another intriguing twist in his relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — his partner in theIran war,which threatens GOP hopes in Tuesday’s midterm elections. And it comes at a critical political moment, with Israel in political limbo after there was no clear winner inlast week’s electionand uncertainty over Netanyahu’s future.

The political dynamic in the US is also impossible to ignore. In a sense, Trump seems to be conceding a point to Democrats such as Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed in implying that aid to Israel is becoming politically unsustainable in US politics.

This underscores an extraordinary fracture in the long-lasting bipartisan pro-Israel consensus in Washington.

And it goes beyond the question of how a new Democratic House or Senate would handle the issue after Tuesday’s midterms. The announcement points to an uncertain new era for Israel: Netanyahu has been aligned with Republicans in Washington through several administrations, but there has been significantdomestic backlashto Netanyahu’s response in Gaza to the October 7, 2023, Hamas terror attacks, not only among progressives but also activistson the rightof Trump’s MAGA movement.

Growing uncertainty over whether there will be a congressional majority to back Israel and arms sales to its military will create huge future geopolitical implications for the Jewish state and US Middle East policy.

Trump loves to shock, to create news around himself and to distract. So perhaps his announcement in an interview on Fox News was a political play on a day when many Republicans feara stinging rebuke from voters.

He certainly seemed to surprise the Fox anchors.

“I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping …. they’re fine with it because, you know, they’ve become a very successful country,” he said. Trump added that the US would help the Israelis if they needed it. “But by end of this year, we won’t be paying Israel.”

The president appeared to be referring to annual US military aid to Israel, which amounts to just less than $4 billion a yearunder a dealmade under former President Barack Obama in 2016. That arrangement is due to runthrough the end of 2028.

Most of the funds are spent on buying weapons and equipment for the Israeli armed forces from exclusively US manufacturers, so the deal has significant implications for US businesses and employment. Attention is turning to what US and Israeli military cooperation will look like in future. Netanyahu told the Economist in January he wanted to “taper off” US military aid to Israeli within 10 years and that the shift was “in the works.”

It’s hard to know whether Trump’s statement on Tuesday means that the US aid would stop immediately, a step that would be intriguing but would not amount to a strategic fracture between the allies. Foreign policy analysts who have served in both Republican and Democratic administrations have argued Israel is now such a powerful economy that it doesn’t need US aid to buy military equipment. The nexus between US arms manufacturers and Israel is expected to remain strong, and the militaries of the allies have recently worked together more closely than ever. That was the case even before the Iran war — for instance, when theBiden administrationstaged massive air and naval defensive operations to repel Iranian cruise missile and drone attacks in 2024.

Brett McGurk, who was a senior White House and State Department official for four administrations, said the issue of US aid to Israel is deeply misunderstood. “I wouldn’t overstate the significance” of Trump’s remarks Tuesday, McGurk said.

“Whether he’s talking about, we’re going to end the MOU when it ends in 2028, or we’re going to stop it right now, I don’t know,” added McGurk, a CNN global affairs analyst and author of the new book “Brink” about his role negotiating hostage releases in the Gaza crisis.

Trump’s announcement came as tens of millions of Americans are voting after an election campaign that showcased the new intertwining of the issue of Israel and the Palestinians in domestic US politics.

It was extraordinary to hear him apparently reacting to opposition to US aid to Israel from Democrats like El-Sayed, whom he’s subjected to atorrent of anti-Muslim rhetoric. The Michigan Democrat has argued that Americans are paying more for groceries because of a war the US is fighting at the behest of Israel.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they (Israel) don’t need it?” Trump told Fox and Friends. “It’s a bad talking point because you’d say — ‘Why don’t we give everybody $4 billion?’”

The Israel issue caused a weekend clash between El-Sayed and his former Democratic primary foeHaley Stevens, who then endorsed his GOP rival, Mike Rogers. Stevens objected to an ad by a left-wing influencer featuring a couple in a supermarket blaming higher prices on Israel. El-Sayed denounced the ad, which his team said was not affiliated with the campaign. But the showdown encapsulated the schism over Israel that could complicate any new Democratic congressional majorities.

Progressives may interpret Trump’s shift as a validation of their positions. “Even a broken clock can be right twice a day,” El-Sayed said Tuesday, according to theWall Street Journal. Others, however, argue that critiques of Israel’s government too often cross over into antisemitism — a charge candidates like El-Sayed deny.

Trump may also be seeking a political win for himself. Ending US aid to Israel would speak to Trump’s “America First” instincts and hostility to the use of American wealth to support foreign nations. His argument that he’d use unspent cash to pay down the deficit is less convincing, given ballooning national debt in his two terms.

While progressives are outraged at Israel because of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, anti-Israel sentiment has also been rising to Trump’s right in the Republican Party, fanned by influencers and podcasters with huge audiences. CNN’s Donie O’Sullivan, who has spent monthsspeaking with Trump supporters, found many believe the US is fighting Israel and are skeptical about the US relationship with its government.

In aQuinnipiac pollpublished in June, 48% of respondents said the US is too supportive of Israel; 38% said US support was about right; and only 7% said the US was not supportive enough. This was the highest percentage of voters thinking that Washington was too supportive of Israel since Quinnipiac first started asking the question in January 2017.

In a sign of how sentiment on Israel has shifted among Democrats, former Obama White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, who may run for president in 2028, has argued against unconditional US military aid to Israel and called for a new US relationship with the country in aspeech in Tel Avivearlier this year.

In one sense, it might make sense politically for Israel to try to separate its military decisions and purchases from polarizing US domestic politics. It would be free to make its own choices about what to buy, although in practice it’s unlikely to turn to Europe’s manufacturers because of huge public anger there over Gaza. The idea that it would purchase Russian or Chinese equipment seems a long shot given certain US opposition.

But such scenarios point to another headache for Israel if it remains a flashpoint in US politics. Presidents can authorize arms sales to foreign states; lawmakers can seek to block them, but in this case, the chances of veto-proof majorities seem slim.

But there’s another worrying possibility for Israel’s supporters: that political hostility produces a president from either party who is less committed to its national security needs than Trump, former President Joe Biden or their predecessors.

As Emanuel put it in an interview with CNN’s Fareed Zakaria in July, Israel could pay a price because of its own actions. “That’s not a Democratic Party problem. That’s an America problem,” he said.
